On social media, Prime Minister Narendra Modi was quick to call the numbers proof of the country’s “collective strength”, aiming a pointed remark at “doomsayers” along the way, while also urging people to avoid travelling abroad for leisure, host weddings overseas, and refrain from buying gold. Meanwhile, the Congress pushed back, flagging weak agricultural growth, a sluggish manufacturing sector, job creation and rising debt. Into this contest of narratives, NDTV invited Subhash Chandra Garg, India’s former finance secretary, for an interview with anchor Gaurie Dwivedi. items.title: Rationalising legal fees: The AI conundrum for law firms and their clients
items.summary: Indian law firms are already using artificial intelligence (AI) and clients have started asking for their bills to reflect that. At a panel in New Delhi on August 17 , Hyundai Motor India's General Counsel Amitabh Lal Das said that law firms should bill fewer hours once AI lets them finish research faster . Das said he had, in his own experience, been charged research fees disproportionate to the advice produced and that he expected AI adoption to bring down companies' external legal spending generally. The instinct behind cutting the bill because the work got faster is understandable. It is also the wrong place to start. A blanket discount treats every hour of AI-assisted work as equally cheapened, when the truth is closer to what Senior Advocate Chander Uday Singh raised at the same panel: generative tools occasionally invent case law that was never delivered and shape answers around what the questioner wants to hear rather than what the law actually holds, a tendency juniors are least equipped to catch. The real answer to Das's demand does not sit in a percentage knocked off in an invoice. It sits inside every firm's own time-sheets. Das's concern is the saving created by faster research. Singh's concern is what happens between an AI-generated answer and the advice an advocate is actually prepared to sign. Neither position is wrong, but taken alone, each creates a problem: Das's view gives a client no basis for sizing the discount it wants and Singh's view leaves a firm treating every AI output with the same suspicion, whether or not it deserves it. What has actually changed A legal fee has traditionally bundled 3 things into one rate: legal research, the professional judgment involved in choosing which defensible position to advise on and the risk of signing that advice. These were hard to price separately, so the billable hour stood in for all three. Generative tools can now perform a substantial part of the research function and have left judgment largely untouched, since telling a sound conclusion apart from a merely fluent one is exactly what these systems do least reliably. They have also created a new task: checking the machine's output before it reaches a client or a court. That task does not appear on any Indian invoice as a line of its own. The firm's experience has not become less valuable; what has changed is the cost of producing the first draft. items.title: Driving at high speed alone not rash or negligent driving: Delhi High Court
items.summary: Vehicles are intended to be driven fast and the fact that a vehicle was moving at high speed does not, by itself, establish criminal rashness or negligence on the part of the driver, the Delhi High Court recently observed [State v Sanjay] . Justice Chandrasekharan Sudha made the observation while dismissing the Delhi government’s appeal against the acquittal of a tempo driver booked under Sections 279 (rash driving) and 304A (causing death by negligence) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for causing a woman’s death in a road accident in 2009. “ Vehicles are intended to be driven in speed. Merely because the vehicle was driven at high speed would not mean that the driver was rash or negligent by itself. ‘High speed’ or ‘over speed’ are relative terms, ” the Court said. Justice Chandrasekharan Sudha Delhi High Court Merely because the vehicle was driven at high speed would not mean that the driver was rash or negligent by itself. The case arose from an accident on November 12, 2009. The prosecution alleged that the accused was driving a tempo rashly and negligently when it struck a bicycle carrying a man and his mother near Naresh Park Extension in Delhi. The tempo’s front wheel allegedly ran over the woman’s head, killing her on the spot. A magistrate acquitted the driver in August 2013. The State challenged the decision before the High Court in 2016. The deceased woman’s son, who was riding the bicycle, was the prosecution’s sole witness. He testified that the tempo was being driven at a very high speed and in a rash and negligent manner. However, the High Court found that he did not explain how the driving was rash or negligent. He was also unable to give even an approximate estimate of the tempo’s speed. “ Mere occurrence of a road traffic incident, which results in a fatality, cannot ipso facto lead to an inference of rashness or negligence on the part of the driver, ” the Court said. The prosecution was required to produce material explaining what constituted high speed in the circumstances of the case, the Court added. In the absence of such material, rashness or negligence could not be presumed by applying the principle of res ipsa loquitur . The Court also highlighted inconsistencies in the prosecution’s case. items.title: Elephants have rights: Karnataka High Court quashes land acquisition for housing project near Bannerghatta
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court has quashed the acquisition of over 1,938 acres of land for the 4th phase of Suryanagar housing project by Karnataka Housing Board (KHB), holding that the project would have irreversible ecological and wildlife-related consequences [Puttarajamma v State of Karnataka] . A division bench of Justices DK Singh and H Shanthi Bhushan passed the judgment while allowing the appeals filed by the landowners against the acquisition of their agricultural land for Suryanagar 4th Phase Layout. The Court observed that while the Suryanagar project seeks to provide affordable and planned housing plots, it would deprive the wildlife of their natural habitat. It added that the project would seriously affect the Karadikkal-Madeshwara Corridor for elephants. “The elephants in question, for whom these corridors constitute not merely a passage but an essential part of their natural habitat and existence, cannot be treated as occupants without rights whose homes may be displaced at will,” the Bench said. Justice DK Singh and Justice H Shanthi Bhushan Karnataka High Court Elephants in question cannot be treated as occupants without rights. Accordingly, the Court set aside the decision of a single-bench, which had only partly interfered with the acquisition of land on January 13, 2025. "The entire land acquisition proceedings are nothing but an exercise without undertaking the relevant considerations such as, scientific study of environment impact assessment, socio-ecological factors etc., as flagged by the CEC," the Court ruled. The KHB had initially proposed acquisition of 2,220 acres and two guntas. Following objections by landowners, the State in 2015 issued notifications covering 1,938 acres and 13 guntas. The project involved the acquisition of land in Konasandra, Bommandahalli, Kadujakkanahalli, Indlawadi and Bagganadoddi villages in Anekal taluk. State Environment Impact Assessment Authority granted clearance for the project in 2023. However, the decision was challenged by landowners who, among other things, argued that their agricultural land was the source of their livelihood. It was also argued that the acquisition raised serious environmental concerns in view of the project's proximity to Bannerghatta National Park. A Division Bench of Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia asked the petitioner, Gopala Krishna Kosaraju, to agitate his grievance before the Andhra Pradesh High Court. Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia The old Visakhapatnam airport at INS Dega, which had handled scheduled commercial flights for decades, ceased such operations last month. The shutdown followed the inauguration of the new Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport at Bhogapuram on August 1. All scheduled passenger flights were transferred to the new airport, while INS Dega remains available for non-scheduled and military operations. Advocate Pranav Sachdeva appeared for the petitioner and argued that the new airport is nearly 60 Km from the city of Visakhapatnam and takes over two hours to reach. "There is no connectivity, and the people are suffering. The existing airport was built with thousands of crores of rupees," he said. items.title: Bombay High Court sets aside alimony order issued based on guesswork of husband's income
items.summary: The Bombay High Court recently quashed a Pune family court order granting ₹10 lakhs as permanent alimony to a woman, after finding the family court based its decision purely on "guesswork" of her estranged husband’s income. In the absence of proper income details, he family court judge had assumed that the husband earned ₹1 lakh per month since he was a skilled and qualified person who had earlier worked in Germany. A Division Bench of Justices Bharati Dangre and Ashish S Chavan strongly disapproved of this approach, observing that the family court judge had carried out such guesswork without any evidence. "The learned Judge has merely carried out a guess work without any evidence produced on record as to what is the earning of the husband and what is the need of the wife," the High Court observed. Justices Bharati Dangre and Ashish S Chavan The High Court, therefore, remanded the matter back to the family court for fresh adjudication. It directed the family court judge to determine the amount of permanent alimony by drawing a statement of the earnings of the husband and the needs of the wife. “ We deem it appropriate to remand the matter back to the Judge, Family Court, Pune, for determination of the amount of permanent alimony as well as the amount of maintenance to be paid to the daughter, which would necessarily have to be commensurate with the earnings of the appellant since the learned Judge has merely carried out a guess work without any evidence produced on record as to what is the earning of the husband and what is the need of the wife,” the Court ordered. The husband had approached the family court with a plea for divorce on the grounds of cruelty. The wife had not defended the case. The court had dissolved the marriage and directed the husband to pay ₹10 lakh as permanent alimony. It also ordered ₹10,000 per month for child maintenance. The husband filed a plea before the High Court challenging the financial directions. He objected to the manner in which the family court had speculated on how much he was earning as income. “ In absence of details, it can be assumed that the petitioner's net income must be ₹1 lakh a month," the family court had ruled. The High Court bench found this approach unacceptable. It stated that permanent alimony and maintenance would have to be commensurate with the actual earnings of the husband. items.title: Delhi High Court seeks response from State, MCD on PIL flagging lack of burial spaces for Christians
items.summary: The Delhi High Court on Wednesday issued notice to the Delhi government, Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) and Delhi Development Authority (DDA) on a plea highlighting lack of cemeteries and burial grounds for Christians. A Division Bench of Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia observed that under the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, one of the functions assigned to the MCD is to regulate and maintain places meant for disposal of the dead. “It thus appears that it is one of the primary functions assigned to MCD to arrange for spaces where the citizens of the city can observe last rites such as burial grounds and cemeteries," the Court said. Therefore, it directed the MCD to give details of the Christian cemeteries/burial grounds within its territorial jurisdiction and also the space available for the said purpose. The matter will be heard next on November 4. Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia The Court passed the order while dealing with a public interest litigation (PIL) petition filed by Legal Christians Action Committee (petitioner). The petitioner sought directions to the authorities to identify and allot suitable land in Delhi for a Christian cemetery, citing an acute shortage of burial grounds in the national capital. According to the plea, existing Christian cemeteries at Burari, Patel Chest, Paharganj, Mangolpuri and Prithviraj Road are old and have reached full capacity. As a result, families are allegedly being forced to transport the mortal remains of deceased relatives to neighbouring states, including Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh, for burial. The petitioner said it had been approaching the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) and Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) since June 2025, including through representations and an RTI application, but no concrete action has been taken. Further, the plea added that the DDA had identified three potential sites at Khajuri Khas, near Rajiv Gandhi Hospital and Sundar Nagri. While the latter two were subsequently ruled out, Khajuri Khas was taken up for processing. However, the petitioner was later informed that the Khajuri Khas land was unavailable for allotment. The PIL petition before the High Court was filed through advocates Nagmani Kumar and Abhinav Kumar.

items.title: Mozambican and Indian companies move Delhi HC alleging ICC arbitrator did not disclose conflict of interest
items.summary: A Mozambican and an Indian company have approached the Delhi High Court challenging a partial award passed by an International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) arbitral tribunal. They have alleged that the presiding arbitrator failed to disclose material appointments and past criminal proceedings against him. The petitions, filed by Black Gold Resources Private Limitada (BGR) and Trident Chemphar Limited (TCL), have challenged the tribunal’s 2:1 decision to include TCL to the arbitration between BGR and Minas De Benga Limitada (MDB) despite being a non-signatory to the contract. The dispute arose from a Mozambican coal mining contract. The Tribunal was presided over by Professor Sundra Rajoo . Former Supreme Court Justice L Nageswara Rao and one DK Singh were co-arbitrators. On May 5 this year, the tribunal delivered a split verdict. While Professor Rajoo and Justice Rao held that TCL, BGR’s Indian shareholder, could be brought into the arbitration, Singh dissented. BGR and TCL then approached the High Court. Justice Sachin Datta heard the challenge today and issued notices to MDB and said that the matter will be heard in October. Senior Advocate Abhimanyu Mahajan , representing TCL, argued that the case reflected an institutional failure by the ICC. Senior Advocate Amit Sibal appeared for BGR and highlighted the alleged bias on part of the president. He said that their submission was rejected by the arbitral tribunal without engagement. “We cited Mozambican law and in one word the tribunal rejected it,” Sibal stated. Meanwhile, Senior Advocate Rajshekhar Rao appeared for MDB. He argued that the ICC has rejected the petitioners’ challenge to the appointment of the presiding arbitrator though a formal communication is yet to be issued. Rao added that in view of the allegations made against the President, Justice L Nageswar Rao has also recused. He opposed passing of any interim order in the case. After hearing the lawyers, Justice Datta said that since Justice Rao has recused from the proceedings, the tribunal is effectively not functioning. items.title: Madras High Court sets aside ban on temples acquiring elephants
items.summary: The Madras High Court on Wednesday set aside a single-judge’s direction prohibiting temples in Tamil Nadu from acquiring elephants [Arulmigu Sri Subramania Swami Thirukoil vs Sheik Mohammed]. A Bench of Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G Arul Murugan held that the direction travelled beyond the case concerning a female elephant, and affected temples that were neither parties to the proceedings nor were given an opportunity to be heard. The Court, however, affirmed all directions issued for the custody of the elephant, Lalitha, her medical treatment, retirement and welfare. The Division Bench said that a court exercising writ jurisdiction must ordinarily confine the relief to the pleadings and the parties before it. “ This is not a technicality. It is the very foundation of a fair hearing. However well-intentioned a direction may be, it cannot be sustained if it is passed against persons who were strangers to the proceeding and who had no opportunity to place their case before the court ,” the judgment said. CJ SA Dharmadhikari and Justice Arul Murugan The appeals arose from a February 2023 order passed by a single-judge after Lalitha’s health deteriorated. She had suffered multiple falls between December 2022 and February 2023. After personally inspecting her , the single-judge directed that Lalitha be handed over to forest authorities and the District Level Captive Elephant Welfare Committee for treatment. The judge also declared that she had reached the retirement age of 60 and directed that her mahout and his assistant continue to care for her. However, the order went further and directed an inspection of every temple-owned and privately held elephant in Tamil Nadu. It also called upon the government to consider shifting all captive elephants to government rehabilitation camps and directed the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department to instruct temples not to acquire elephants in future. Appeals were then filed by the Tamil Nadu government and the Arulmigu Sri Subramania Swami Temple at Tiruchendur which owned Lalitha. The Division Bench held that the wider directions issued by the single-judge could not be sustained since the original writ petition concerned only the rejection of an application to transfer Lalitha’s ownership. items.title: Supreme Court to consider BCI reconstitution after State Bar elections; AG, SG to be consulted before any BCI decision
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Wednesday ordered that Attorney General (AG) R Venkataramani and Solicitor General (SG) Tushar Mehta actively participate in every decision taken by the Bar Council of India (BCI) [ Yogamaya MG vs. Union of India ]. A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana passed the direction after multiple petitions alleged gross illegality in Senior Advocate Manan Kumar Mishra continuing as chairperson of Bar Council of India (BCI) without authority. "Both the Attorney General for India and the Solicitor General for India shall be actively associated with every policy decision taken by the Bar Council of India," the Court directed. However, the issue of Mishra's chairmanship and whether the BCI needs to be reconstituted, will be considered only after elections to all State Bar Councils conclude and they elect their representatives to the BCI. Justice Joymalya Bagchi, CJI Surya Kant and Justice V Mohana Thus, the Court did not pass any adverse directions against Mishra today but said it will await the completion of State Bar Council elections and then take a call on the issue of BCI's reconstitution. Pertinently, Justice Bagchi remarked that it was apparent from the facts of the case that Mishra can continue as chairperson only till a fresh election is held. " We are not placing any stamp of approval upon the existing arrangement. It is apparent that the present chairperson can continue only until a fresh election to the Bar Council of India takes place pursuant to the State Bar Council elections already conducted. The new State Bar Councils are about to be constituted and the election contemplated under Section 4(1)(c) must then take place. In such situations, day-to-day functioning can be left to the existing arrangement. However, when a policy decision is taken, the participation of a permanent ex officio member acting independently, such as the Attorney General, is necessary," Justice Bagchi orally said. items.title: What India’s reservation debate tells us about the scarcity of opportunity
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. After the recent student movement led by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) over failures in the examination system, Delhi’s Jantar Mantar has housed another andolan: the Reservation Hatao Andolan. An online campaign that reportedly crossed 5.6 million Instagram followers has brought anti-reservation frustration into public view. Some protesters have said they are not against reservation as such, but believe eligibility should be determined by people’s financial condition. The movement, however, has broadly campaigned for the removal of caste-based reservations. The demand raises a familiar question: who should get a scarce opportunity? But the more important question here is why opportunities have become scarce enough for their allocation to generate such intense group competition. India’s reservation debate is partly a debate about scarcity. When limited jobs, educational seats, and public resources are allocated through socially salient categories, competition can acquire a zero-sum character in which one group’s gain is perceived as another’s loss. The answer is neither to dismiss redistribution nor to assume that growth will resolve the problem. It is to address historical discrimination while expanding the institutions and opportunities over which citizens compete. More students, limited mobility India’s higher education has expanded considerably. Total enrolment rose from 3.42 crore in 2014-15 to 4.46 crore in 2022-23, while the gross enrolment ratio for 18-23-year-olds rose from 23.7% in 2014-15 to 30% in 2023-24. SC enrolment increased by about 50% and ST enrolment by about 75% between 2014-15 and 2022-23. But more students do not automatically mean more pathways to secure employment. A degree from a well-resourced institution with strong faculty, networks, and placement opportunities is not equivalent to a degree from a poorly equipped college. The labour market reflects this gap. The 2025 PLFS puts unemployment among 15-29-year-olds at 9.9%, rising to 13.6% in urban areas. Only 23.6% of workers were in regular wage or salaried employment, while 56.2% were self-employed. These numbers tell a more specific story than a simple job shortage. They show something more specific: education is expanding faster than access to the secure and desirable employment that many young people expect education to provide. items.title: Picked up for speaking Bengali: Inside Bengaluru’s Operation Mukta | TNM Ground Report
items.summary: On August 8, hundreds of migrant workers were picked up from settlements across Bengaluru as part of the Karnataka government’s Operation Mukta, a drive to identify undocumented immigrants. For many Bengali-speaking workers, however, the exercise felt less like verification and more like a detention drive. Workers from West Bengal told TNM that police took them to stations and other facilities, checked their Aadhaar and voter IDs, and in several cases went through their phones, including call logs, messages, photographs, and videos. Some said they were assaulted, while others were separated for further questioning because they had made phone calls to relatives in Bangladesh. One worker, Farooq SK, said police initially told them they would be released within minutes after their documents were checked. Instead, they were taken for biometric verification and kept waiting for hours. Police also checked their phones repeatedly. “Phones have personal matters,” he said. “The police take the phones and go through them.” The operation came after months of growing attention around alleged Bangladeshi illegal immigration in Bengaluru. Hindutva activists and social media influencers have repeatedly targeted Bengali-speaking migrant workers, alleging that they are undocumented Bangladeshis. For instance, Hindutva activist Puneeth Kerehalli has publicly confronted migrant workers and accused them of being Bangladeshi. His claims have also been amplified by television news coverage and social media. Activists say this has created an atmosphere in which Bengali-speaking workers are viewed with suspicion even when they are Indian citizens. Legal researcher Darshana Mitra of the National Law School of India University pointed out that West Bengal, Assam, and Bangladesh share linguistic and cultural overlaps. People living near the border may also have family members across it. Yet, she said, the distinction was being flattened into “Bengali-speaking Muslim equals Bangladeshi”. Activists who visited some of the settlements described people being packed into halls and asked to establish that they were Indian citizens. PUCL’s Aishwarya R said the process was arbitrary, with police also checking private phone data and treating calls to Bangladeshi numbers as grounds for further scrutiny.
